title: From Parts to Patterns: The Mental Tools of Systems Thinking
author: Nicole
source: The Critical Path / PM Researcher (Substack), May 17, 2026
summary: Nicole of The Critical Path lays out six mental movements that define systems thinking as a discipline of attention rather than just a toolkit: from disconnection to interconnectedness, from linear to circular causation, from silos to emergence, from parts to wholes, from analysis to synthesis, and from isolation to relationships. She argues that systems thinking is not a replacement for analytical thinking but a frame that must come before it in complex situations: before you break something into parts, you need a sense of the whole and the relationships that matter. A seventh foundational tool underlies all six movements — the ability to choose the right system boundary, since the boundary drawn around a problem determines what can be seen. The article frames systems thinking as the practice of asking better questions rather than applying prebuilt diagrams.
points: Systems thinking should often precede analytical thinking in complex situations — analysis needs direction; without a systems frame, you risk measuring what is easy to isolate rather than what actually matters.

The circular causation movement is among the most practically important: systems respond to interventions, feedback loops reinforce or balance patterns, and a solution that works once may fail later because the system has changed in response.

Emergence — what appears when parts interact — is difficult precisely because it challenges blame: many outcomes arise not from one broken part but from the structure of interaction among parts, which no single person controls.
Synthesis is not summary; it is the act of forming a coherent understanding from complexity, bringing the detail from analysis back into a unified picture of what the whole is doing and why.
Choosing the right boundary is a judgment skill, not a technical one: the boundary determines the story, and drawing it too narrow or too wide will make the real pattern invisible.
quotes: Some problems cannot be understood only by taking them apart. Their behavior comes from relationships, feedback, timing, incentives, assumptions, and interactions. The issue is not always in the parts themselves. Sometimes the issue is in the pattern the parts are creating together.

This is why a solution may work once and fail later. The system has changed in response to the solution. Circular thinking helps us notice feedback. Some feedback reinforces a pattern. The more something happens, the more it continues to happen. Trust builds trust. Mistrust builds mistrust.

Emergence is difficult because it challenges blame. It suggests that outcomes may arise not from one broken part, but from the structure of interaction itself. A group may have capable individuals and still produce confusion. A process may have well-defined steps and still create delays.

Systems thinking should often come before analytical thinking in complex situations. Before we break a problem into pieces, we need some sense of the whole. Without a systems frame, analysis can become fragmentation. We may analyze the wrong parts.

The way we draw the boundary shapes what we can see. Draw the boundary around one task, and the problem may look like execution. Draw it around incentives, and it may look like behavior. Draw it around time, and it may look like a feedback loop. The boundary determines the story.

Systems thinking is often presented as a set of tools: diagrams, maps, loops, models, and frameworks. These tools matter. They help make invisible patterns visible. But before systems thinking becomes a diagram, it is a discipline of attention.
